# Code review iteration

Reviewed the whole repository at commit `efe80d1 2023-12-28`: the Go stub sources (`module.go`, `integration.go`, tests), `go.mod`/`go.sum`, `tools/`, the Makefile and Taskfile with the `bin/lib` bash library, `.golangci.yml`, all `.github/workflows/*`, the composite notify action, Dependabot and Probot settings, and the Nextra docs site. The angle: this is a GitHub TEMPLATE repository, so tooling defaults, pinned versions, and CI wiring are the product — every defect here propagates into each repository generated from it. Reviewed against the Go 1.26-era ecosystem. `.github/issues/` and `.github/roadmap/` were ignored as offline backlog dumps. No previous files existed in `.github/reviews/`, so all findings below are new.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Script injection via the head commit message in the notify composite action

`.github/actions/notify/action.yml:26-46`

```yaml
(cat <<-message
txt=${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}
message
) | head -1 >> $GITHUB_OUTPUT
```

`${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}` (and `${{ github.event.inputs.reason }}` below it) is expanded by the Actions runner *before* the shell parses the script. A commit message containing a `message` line followed by `); arbitrary command; (cat <<-message` breaks out of the heredoc and executes attacker-chosen shell in the job. This is not theoretical for this repo: `ci.yml` calls the action on every `push` to `main`, squash-merge commit messages are derived from PR titles/bodies (attacker-influenced), and every job first runs `actions/checkout` with default `persist-credentials: true` and `fetch-depth: 0` — so injected code can read the `GITHUB_TOKEN` out of `.git/config` and act with its permissions. This is the canonical "untrusted input in run step" pattern GitHub's security lab warns about, and the template stamps it into every generated repository. The unquoted `>> $GITHUB_OUTPUT` is a lesser cousin of the same sloppiness.

**Fix.** Never interpolate event payload text into script bodies. Pass it through the environment instead: `env: { COMMIT_MSG: "${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}" }` and then `printf 'txt=%s\n' "$(head -1 <<<"$COMMIT_MSG")" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"`. Apply the same treatment to `inputs.reason` and `workflow_run.name`, and quote `"$GITHUB_OUTPUT"`.

## 2. Template-wide toolchain and dependency rot across Go, linters, actions, and the docs stack

`go.mod:3`, `Makefile:5`, `tools/go.mod:3-12`, `.golangci.yml:1-19`, `.github/workflows/*`, `docs/package.json:9-14`

Everything is frozen at December 2023, and since the repository is a template, every new project inherits the rot on day one. The individual items, folded into one migration list:

- `go.mod` declares `go 1.11` and CI/Makefile pledge a 1.11–1.21 support matrix. In the Go 1.26 era the community standard is the last two releases; the 1.11 pledge is already nominal, not real — `golang.org/x/time v0.5.0` declares `go 1.18`, so pre-1.18 toolchains build it on a best-effort basis only, and one routine Dependabot bump of any dependency will break the old matrix. The pledge also taxes the code itself: the `req.WithContext` dance in `integration.go:22-23` and the redundant `// +build` line in `integration_test.go:2` exist only because of it (`http.NewRequestWithContext` is Go 1.13, `//go:build`-only is fine from 1.17).
- `tools/go.mod` pins `golangci-lint v1.55.2`. golangci-lint is now on v2 with an incompatible config schema (`version: "2"`); of the linters enabled in `.golangci.yml`, `exportloopref` is deprecated and removed (superseded by `copyloopvar` after the Go 1.22 loopvar change, which also obsoletes the `--enable looppointer` in `Makefile:207`), `gosimple` was folded into `staticcheck`, and `typecheck` is no longer an enableable linter.
- `github.com/golang/mock` was archived in June 2023 — before this commit was even made. Its maintained fork is `go.uber.org/mock`.
- The `tools/tools.go` blank-import pattern is superseded by the `tool` directive in `go.mod` (Go 1.24+): `go get -tool`, `go tool golangci-lint`. That removes the entire `tools` module, its 200-line indirect block, and the `go-tools-*` Makefile machinery.
- `codecov/codecov-action@v3.1.4` (`ci.yml:117`) is deprecated; v3's tokenless upload path no longer works reliably. Current is v5 with an explicit `CODECOV_TOKEN`.
- `cloudflare/pages-action@v1.5.0` (`cd.docs.cfp.yml`) is deprecated in favor of `cloudflare/wrangler-action` with `wrangler pages deploy`.
- All actions are minor-pinned at their December 2023 releases (`checkout@v4.1.1`, `setup-go@v5.0.0`, `setup-node@v4.0.1`, `stale@v9.0.0`, …); most have had major releases since. With Dependabot already watching `github-actions`, pin majors (or full SHAs for the security-sensitive ones) instead of stale minors.
- `.github/settings.yml` targets the Probot Settings app, which the README itself footnotes as deprecated. Its replacement (repository rulesets / IaC via Terraform or the gh API) should be decided, not "someday".
- The docs stack is Nextra 2 on Next.js 14 pages router; Nextra 4 requires the App Router and current Next. The `docs/` scaffold needs a deliberate migration, not a version bump.
- `Makefile:96` defaults `GOPROXY=direct`, opting every generated project out of proxy.golang.org caching and availability. That was a defensible 2019 choice; today the default proxy is the ecosystem norm.

**Fix.** One modernization pass: `go 1.25`/`go 1.26` directive plus `toolchain`; support matrix = last two Go releases; drop the 1.11 compatibility code and `// +build` lines; adopt the go.mod `tool` directive and delete `tools/`; regenerate `.golangci.yml` for golangci-lint v2 with `copyloopvar`; swap mockgen to `go.uber.org/mock`; bump codecov to v5 with a token, replace the Cloudflare action, refresh or SHA-pin all actions; decide the settings.yml successor; plan the Nextra 4 migration; drop `GOPROXY=direct`.

## 3. Replace directives pin personal forks of golangci-lint and x tools, neutralizing Dependabot

`tools/go.mod:14-17`

```
replace (
	github.com/golangci/golangci-lint => github.com/kamilsk/golangci-lint v1.55.2
	golang.org/x/tools => github.com/kamilsk/go-tools v0.16.1
)
```

Two problems compound here. First, `replace` pins concrete fork versions, so the Dependabot `gomod` watcher on `/tools/` (configured in `.github/dependabot.yml`) is decorative: it will bump the `require` lines, the `replace` will keep winning, and the installed binaries never change — silent no-op updates, forever. Second, `make lint` depends on fork-only behavior (`--enable looppointer` in `Makefile:207` only exists in the kamilsk fork), so a template consumer who innocently removes the replaces or installs upstream golangci-lint gets a broken `lint` target. A template must not make its default quality gate depend on one person's unmaintained forks of the linter and of `golang.org/x/tools` — that is both a maintenance dead end and a supply-chain liability for every generated project.

**Fix.** Delete both `replace` directives, install upstream golangci-lint (v2), and drop `--enable looppointer` — the Go 1.22 loopvar semantics eliminated the class of bug it and `exportloopref` hunted. If a private analyzer is still wanted, ship it as a separate `golangci-lint` plugin or a standalone `go vet -vettool`, not as a fork of the whole linter.

## 4. Ping and PanicOnErr teach panic-driven error handling as library API design

`integration.go:11-27`

```go
func PanicOnErr(err error) {
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
}

func Ping(ctx context.Context, m *Module) bool {
	...
	resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
	PanicOnErr(err)
```

`Ping` returns a bare `bool` and converts every failure — including perfectly ordinary transient network errors from `http.DefaultClient.Do` — into a panic via an *exported* `PanicOnErr` helper. In a library, panicking on expected runtime errors is a hard anti-pattern: callers cannot distinguish "host unreachable" from a programmer bug, and the process dies unless every caller wraps the call in `recover`. Since this file is the template's showcase of "how to write module code", every generated project starts life with a panic-driven error model and an exported panic helper polluting its API surface. Idiomatic Go (today and in 2023) is the same: return `(bool, error)` or just `error`, and reserve `panic` for invariant violations.

**Fix.** Change the signature to `func Ping(ctx context.Context, m *Module) error` (or `(bool, error)`), propagate errors with `%w` wrapping, and delete `PanicOnErr` from the exported API — if a must-helper is wanted for `main`-adjacent code, keep it unexported in a test or example. The integration test then asserts on the returned error instead of `recover`.

## 5. Ping ignores the HTTP status code and uses the shared default client without a timeout

`integration.go:25-38`

Three concrete correctness gaps in the same ten lines:

- `resp.StatusCode` is never checked. A 404 or 500 flows straight into the XML decoder; an empty error body makes `decoder.Decode` return `io.EOF`, which `PanicOnErr` turns into a panic (see finding 4), and a non-XML body panics likewise.
- `http.DefaultClient` has no timeout. If the caller passes `context.Background()` — exactly what `integration_test.go:15` does — a stalled server hangs the call indefinitely (bounded only by the 1–5 s `-timeout` of `go test`, which then kills the whole test process with a panic dump instead of failing one test).
- `http.NewRequest` + `req.WithContext` (lines 20-23) is the pre-1.13 form kept alive only by the go 1.11 pledge; `http.NewRequestWithContext` has been the idiom for six years, and the repo even enables the `noctx` linter that exists to enforce it.

**Fix.** Use `http.NewRequestWithContext`, a dedicated `http.Client{Timeout: ...}` (or accept a client/doer for testability), check `resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK` before decoding, and return errors instead of panicking. Give the integration test a `context.WithTimeout`.

## 6. The lint gate is hollow because fast true silently drops the heavyweight linters

`.golangci.yml:2`

```yaml
linters:
  fast: true
  enable:
    - errcheck
    - gosimple
    ...
    - staticcheck
```

In golangci-lint v1, `linters.fast: true` does not mean "be quick" — it means "run only the linters marked *fast* from the enabled set". The heavyweight analyzers this config carefully enables — `staticcheck`, `gosimple`, `unused`, and friends — are not fast linters, so they are silently skipped on every `make lint` and every CI run. The gate looks strict on paper and is close to a no-op in practice, and the template propagates that false confidence to every generated repo. (In golangci-lint v2 the global `fast` option was removed precisely because of this confusion.)

**Fix.** Delete `fast: true`. If lint time ever matters, rely on golangci-lint's cache or split a quick pre-commit profile from the full CI profile explicitly — never by silently discarding the analyzers you enabled. Verify after the change with `golangci-lint linters` that the expected set is actually active.

## 7. Workflows run without least-privilege token permissions

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:36` (also `tools.yml`, `warmup.caches.yml`, `cleanup.caches.yml`, `cd.vanity.yml`, and the `build`/`notify` jobs of both docs workflows)

No workflow in the repository declares a top-level `permissions:` block; only the Pages/stale jobs that *elevate* rights declare them. Every other job — linting, testing, notifying — runs with whatever the repository default grants the `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which for older repos and unconfigured orgs is still read-write on everything. Combined with finding 1 (script injection in the notify path) this turns a Slack-message bug into potential repo compromise. Current GitHub hardening guidance is unambiguous: set `permissions: contents: read` at workflow level and elevate per job only where needed. Notably, `settings.yml` — the template's repo-configuration manifest — does not pin the default workflow token permissions either.

**Fix.** Add `permissions: { contents: read }` at the top of every workflow; keep the existing job-level elevations in `cd.docs.ghp.yml` and `cleanup.stale.yml`. Since this is a template, also document (or automate) setting "Workflow permissions: read-only" in the generated repository settings.

## 8. Undefined uuidgen variable makes go-check and the performance target run every test

`Makefile:215`, `Makefile:272`

```make
go-check:
	$(AT) $(GOTEST) -count=1 -test.run=^$(uuidgen) ./...
...
go-performance-test:
	$(AT) $(GOTEST) -bench=. -run=^$(uuidgen) $(GOTESTFLAGS) $(PACKAGES)
```

`$(uuidgen)` is a *make* variable reference, not a shell command substitution. No variable named `uuidgen` is defined, so it expands to the empty string and the flags become `-test.run=^` / `-run=^` — and the regex `^` matches every test name. The intent (a random pattern matching nothing, i.e. "compile everything, run nothing") is inverted: `go-check`, which is wired as the pre-commit hook (`bin/lib/git/hooks/pre-commit`) and the CI "fast check" step (`ci.yml:91`), actually runs the full test suite with `-count=1`, and `go-performance-test` runs all unit tests alongside the benchmarks. It goes unnoticed only because the stub test suite is tiny; in a real project generated from this template the "fast" pre-commit hook quietly becomes a full test run.

**Fix.** Escape the dollar for the shell — `-test.run='^$$(uuidgen)'` — or simpler and conventional, use the literal never-matching pattern `-test.run='^$$'` (shell sees `^$`, which matches only an empty name). Same for `go-performance-test`'s `-run`.

## 9. Empty GOTAGS makes govulncheck swallow its test flag

`Makefile:149`, `Makefile:287`

```make
go-deps-check:
	$(AT) go mod verify
	$(AT) govulncheck -tags $(GOTAGS) -test ./...
```

`GOTAGS` is only ever set as a target-specific variable on the `go-integration-test*` and `go-tools-install` targets; for `go-deps-check` and `go-tools-check` it is empty. The shell therefore sees `govulncheck -tags -test ./...`, and Go's flag parsing takes `-test` as the *value* of `-tags`. Net effect: the vulnerability scan runs with a bogus build tag named `-test` and with test-code scanning silently disabled — the exact opposite of what the recipe spells. This runs on every `make fast-check` in the lint job (`ci.yml:57`), so CI has been green while scanning less than intended.

**Fix.** Use the `-tags=$(GOTAGS)` form (an empty `-tags=` is harmless) or guard it: `$(if $(GOTAGS),-tags $(GOTAGS))`. Apply to both the root and the `tools` variants.

## 10. The default coverage target runs network-dependent integration tests

`Makefile:415-417`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:96`

```make
test-with-coverage: TIMEOUT=5s
test-with-coverage: go-integration-test-with-coverage
```

The innocuously named `test-with-coverage` — the exact command CI runs for the coverage matrix leg — builds with `-tags integration` and therefore executes `TestIntegration`, which performs a live HTTPS request to the vanity host derived from the module name (`https://go.octolab.org/template/module?go-get=1`). Two consequences. First, the template's own CI is hostage to an external service: DNS hiccup or vanity-host downtime fails the build via a panic (finding 4). Second — worse for a template — after a consumer runs `run init my.new/module`, the module name is rewritten, `Ping` targets `https://my.new/module?go-get=1`, and the very first CI run of the freshly generated repository fails with a panic unless they immediately delete the stub or happen to own a working vanity domain. Out-of-the-box red CI is the most expensive first impression a template can make.

**Fix.** Point `test-with-coverage` at `go-test-with-coverage` (unit only) and give integration coverage its own explicit CI step or workflow, guarded and non-required. Better still, make the stub integration test hermetic with `httptest.Server` so generated projects stay green regardless of DNS.

## 11. The supported Go version list is duplicated across four places with no single source

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:66-78`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:94-97`, `.github/workflows/warmup.caches.yml:23-35`, `Makefile:5`, `tools/go.mod:3`

The 1.11–1.21 matrix is hand-copied in `ci.yml` and `warmup.caches.yml`, mirrored as `GO_VERSIONS` in the Makefile, and echoed once more by the pinned `1.21.x` in the lint/tools jobs and the coverage gates (`if: matrix.go == '1.21.x'` at `ci.yml:94/97/100`). Every Go release requires touching at least four files in lockstep; miss one and, e.g., the coverage report silently stops being produced because the string-equality gate no longer matches any matrix leg. For a template meant to be stamped into dozens of repos, this drift is guaranteed.

**Fix.** Shrink the matrix to the supported window (see finding 2), derive it from one place — e.g. `strategy.matrix` fed by a single reusable workflow, or `go-version-file: go.mod` for the primary leg — and replace the `== '1.21.x'` gates with a matrix flag (`include: [{ go: stable, coverage: true }]`) so bumping Go is a one-line change.

## 12. PHONY declaration mismatch for the integration test target

`Makefile:241-244`

```make
go-integration-test:
	$(AT) $(GOTEST) -race -tags $(GOTAGS) ...
.PHONY: go-test-integration-quick
```

The `.PHONY` line names `go-test-integration-quick`, a target that does not exist, leaving the real `go-integration-test` undeclared. It works only until a file or directory named `go-integration-test` appears in the repo root, at which point make will report it "up to date" and skip the tests — the classic silent-skip failure mode `.PHONY` exists to prevent. Clearly a rename leftover.

**Fix.** Change the line to `.PHONY: go-integration-test`.

## 13. Tests use dot imports and bare FailNow without diagnostics

`module_test.go:6`, `module_test.go:16`, `integration_test.go:11`

Both test files dot-import the package under test (`. "go.octolab.org/template/module"`) and fail via bare `t.FailNow()` with no message. Dot imports are flagged by staticcheck ST1001 and are avoided in modern Go even in `_test` packages — the explicit `module.NewModule()` reads better and never shadows. A bare `FailNow` produces a failure with zero context; the standard idiom is `t.Fatalf("got %d calls, want 1", i)`. These two files are the template's example of "how to write tests here", so the style multiplies.

**Fix.** Import the package by name, replace `t.FailNow()` with `t.Fatalf`/`t.Errorf` carrying got/want detail, and consider `t.Parallel()` in the unit test as the default pattern for consumers to copy.

## 14. The README integration snippet installs the wrong module path

`README.md:183`

```bash
$ go get go.octolab.org@latest
```

`go.octolab.org` is not this module — the module path is `go.octolab.org/template/module`. Anyone following the Integration section gets a resolution error (or a different module entirely). Since the README doubles as the template for generated projects' READMEs, the broken snippet propagates.

**Fix.** `go get go.octolab.org/template/module@latest`, and in the template flow make `run init` rewrite this line together with the module path (today `init` only rewrites `*.go` files, leaving README, badges, and docs pointing at the old module).
